assertions.text: Trigger detection, shipment optimisation, and companion constraint are in separate tables. Not one monolithic table.
assertions.evidence: Five distinct tables: Tables 1-3 cover triggers (Fulfillment Method Split, Availability-Based Grouping, Multiple Delivery Addresses), Table 4 covers shipment optimization (Warehouse Assignment — Minimizing Shipments), and Table 5 covers companion constraint (Companion Product Grouping).

assertions.text: At least one row where multiple triggers fire simultaneously (e.g. mixed fulfilment AND mixed stock status).
assertions.evidence: Each table independently addresses one trigger type. Table 1 shows fulfillment splits only, Table 2 shows availability splits only, Table 3 shows address splits only. No single scenario row demonstrates multiple trigger types firing together (e.g., a row with both different fulfillment methods AND different stock statuses).

assertions.text: All four split triggers are covered: mixed fulfilment, mixed stock status, no single warehouse has all items, different addresses.
assertions.evidence: Mixed fulfillment covered in Table 1 ('One delivery, one pickup'). Mixed stock status covered in Table 2 ('In-stock + pre-order'). No single warehouse has all items covered in Table 4 ('Three warehouses minimum — no two-warehouse option' and 'Two warehouses optimal — avoid three'). Different addresses covered in Table 3 ('Two items, two addresses' and 'Three different addresses').

assertions.text: The 'no warehouse has both companions' case is included and recognised as a product decision — e.g. flagged as an open question, or the chosen resolution is explained. Not silently omitted.
assertions.evidence: Table 5 Row 2 explicitly includes 'No warehouse stocks both companions' scenario. The response contains an open question: 'When companions must split (no warehouse has both), which companion does a non-companion item travel with?'

assertions.text: Companion constraint covers at least: companions at same location, companions split from non-companion items, and the ambiguous case (no location has both).
assertions.evidence: Table 5 Row 1 covers companions at same location ('One warehouse stocks both companions'). Row 3 covers companions split from non-companions ('Companions at one warehouse, non-companion at another'). Row 2 covers no location having both ('No warehouse stocks both companions').

assertions.text: Optimisation scenarios describe the business situation (e.g. 'Consolidate: two beats three', 'Everything at one warehouse') — not 'Test case 2'.
assertions.evidence: Table 4 scenario names describe business situations: 'One warehouse has full stock', 'Two warehouses optimal — avoid three', 'Three warehouses minimum — no two-warehouse option', 'Different items, each at a different warehouse', 'Different items, one warehouse has both'.

assertions.text: The trigger table represents multi-item orders where each item has its own fulfillment type, address, and availability. The notation used makes the item-to-property mapping unambiguous — not value sets like {delivery, pickup} which lose which item has which property.
assertions.evidence: Tables 1-3 use position-based mapping with ordered columns. Example from Table 1: 'Items: Shirt, Shoes | Fulfillment Methods: Delivery, Pickup' clearly maps Shirt to first delivery method and Shoes to second (pickup). No use of ambiguous value sets.

assertions.text: Optimisation table uses a scalar count column (e.g. 'Shirts ordered') not item lists, when product identity doesn't matter for the logic.
assertions.evidence: Table 4 uses 'Qty Needed' as a scalar column (6, 5, 6, 5, 6) with 'Item' specifying what the quantity refers to, rather than listing items as sets.

assertions.text: Inventory assignments are physically valid: items are only assigned to locations that have them. Shipment counts match the assignments shown.
assertions.evidence: Table 4 assignments all match warehouse stock: 'Chicago: 6' (warehouse had 6), 'Philadelphia: 3, Washington: 3' (each had 3 and needed 6 total), 'Chicago: 2, LA: 2, Houston: 1' (quantities match what warehouses stocked).

assertions.text: @DisplayName is present on test methods, OR method names read as clear descriptive titles when converted from camelCase/snake_case.
assertions.evidence: Scenario names throughout tables read as clear descriptive titles: 'One warehouse has full stock', 'Two warehouses optimal — avoid three', 'Multiple delivery items with one pickup'. These would convert clearly to method names satisfying the OR condition.

assertions.text: @Description is present on at least the class and provides context beyond what the table rows already express — such as the splitting rules, constraints, or application context. Does NOT merely restate the column names or summarise what the rows show.
assertions.evidence: No Java @Description annotations are shown in the response. While descriptive text appears before tables ('Items in the same order cannot share a shipment when their fulfillment methods differ'), these are markdown headers, not Java @Description annotations as required by the assertion.

assertions.text: Annotations appear in order: @DisplayName (if present), @Description (if present), @TableTest — not any other order.
assertions.evidence: No Java annotations are present in the response. The response contains markdown tables and descriptive text, but no @DisplayName, @Description, or @TableTest annotations to verify ordering.

assertions.text: If @Description is present and the text is longer than a single short line, it uses a text block (triple-quoted string """), not string concatenation with +. Passes if @Description is absent.
assertions.evidence: @Description annotations are absent from the response, so the default pass condition ('Passes if @Description is absent') is satisfied.
